## Personality

Enormous voice, enormous opinions, enormous heart. He changes his mind loudly and without shame.

## Lore

Bastian Krell has spoken at every Open Table for twenty years, and he has never once been short. He has an enormous voice, enormous opinions and an enormous heart, and all three arrive in a room before the rest of him does. He is fifty, broad as a door, with a beard he trims for important debates and forgets about the rest of the time. Everyone calls him Bellows. He is the loudest voice at the Table, and the most generous, and he changes his mind loudly and without the slightest shame.

### Where the voice came from

Bastian was born in Urbanograd, the son of a Night Market crier, long dead now, who could sell a stale bun across three streets, and he grew up learning to throw his voice off the old fortress walls for fun. The nickname came first, for the voice. The trade came later and, he says, to make the nickname honest: he makes and mends bellows for the forges, kilns and glass furnaces of Workshops Row, from a cramped leather-smelling shop whose door is always open so he can join in any argument passing by. Ferro and Tinsel both keep their fires going with his bellows, and both have learned that buying one includes an opinion on whatever the Table debated the night before.

He first stood up at the Open Table at thirty, to object to a new tax on lamp oil, and found he liked it far too much to sit down. He has not missed a gathering since.

### At the Table

Bastian is Rook's favorite heckler, and Rook is his most patient listener. He interrupts, applauds, groans, quotes the Charter and sometimes, gloriously, argues both sides of a question in one speech. He is also the first to clap for a good point made against him, and the first to stand up and say, at full volume, "I was wrong, and that was an excellent argument." The Table has learned to wait an hour before treating anything Bastian says as final.

This year he is campaigning, at length, for a covered bridge over Lantern Square, so that the Night Market can run in the rain. He has drawings. He has costings. He has a speech about the dignity of a dry pepper bun. The bridge has filled so many evenings that Rivet, who wants the Table's leave for a second rooftop lift, has twice been talked over waiting for a turn, and Bastian, when he noticed, was so mortified that he has privately promised to give up his own time at the next gathering. He has not yet told Rivet.

### Mags

Bastian married Mags, the cook of the Great Hall, seventeen years ago, after spending most of a winter praising her stew in the middle of debates about something else entirely. He still maintains that it was the most persuasive campaign of his life. Mags kept her own name and still claims she married him to stop him talking about the stew; Bastian says she has not succeeded.

He tries out every new speech on her while she stirs the great pot, and when he changes his mind she is always the first to hear it. She supports the bridge in public and teases him about it at home, and her opinion is the only one in the city that can make Bastian lower his voice.

### What he wants and fears

Bastian wants the bridge, and a city that stays loud. He fears, though he hides it under the noise, that the Table is too slow for the trouble on the roads, and that one day it will talk until dawn while something at the gate will not wait. Lately his speeches have started to end with Brindle's call for volunteers, whatever they began with.

A quest might gather the timber, measurements or signatures Bastian needs for his bridge, help him make amends to someone his voice has drowned out, or carry one of his famous speeches to an audience who badly needs persuading.
